strengths: The central theoretical claims are clear and valuable: Theorems 4.1-4.3 formalize why common guidance approximations (posterior mean, Gaussian posterior, and gradient rescaling for tempering) are inconsistent estimators of the diffused likelihood, explaining a known empirical failure mode of DPS/ΠGDM-style methods. The proofs (Jensen-type arguments, convolution argument in A.2) appear essentially sound, and the observation that guidance scales must be applied inside the integral (Eq. 13 vs. Eq. 12) is a genuinely useful clarification that also applies to classifier guidance.

The proposed CBG estimators are principled and consistent: they directly Monte Carlo the integral in Eq. (6), with a differentiable (reparameterization) variant and a gradient-free REINFORCE-style variant that supports non-differentiable rewards. The analysis in Section 5.3 of why the self-normalized gradient-free estimator can have lower variance than the gradient-based one, contrary to standard intuition, is a nice practical contribution.

The Bayesian inference benchmark experiments are convincing and well-designed: using C2ST against reference posterior samples with a controlled compute budget (N·K ≤ 1e5 likelihood evaluations), CBG (grad-free) converges toward the optimal value with increasing compute while baselines plateau, and achieves the best distributional fit on all five tasks, also beating likelihood-free SBI methods on average. This directly supports the paper's central claim.

Application to black hole imaging demonstrates scalability to a real scientific inverse problem with a learned diffusion prior, achieving the best PSNR (26.10) in a standardized benchmark (InverseBench) without computing likelihood gradients.
The paper is clearly written with a helpful motivation figure, and the limitations section honestly acknowledges the compute cost of sampling from p(x|xt).
weaknesses: Originality is moderate: the core method—drawing K samples from the diffusion posterior and reweighting by the likelihood at each step—is a fairly natural Monte Carlo/particle-based idea already partially explored in DCPS (local Monte Carlo updates) and concurrent work (Potaptchik et al., 2026 uses the same estimators of Eqs. (16)/(20)). The novelty rests mainly on the bias theorems and the consistency framing rather than on the algorithm itself.

The claimed connection between calibration and the black hole imaging result is weakly supported: PSNR is a point-estimate fidelity metric and does not measure posterior calibration. There is no assessment of posterior uncertainty or calibration on the scientific task, so the strongest empirical support for calibrated inference comes only from the low-dimensional SBI benchmark.

The gradient-based estimator performs poorly on the higher-dimensional/nonlinear tasks (Table 1: average 0.681, e.g., 0.789 and 0.852 on Tasks 3 and 5), undermining the claim that it is the preferred estimator when gradients are available; in practice only the gradient-free variant is viable, which limits the framework's demonstrated scope.

Practical cost is substantial: K=512 samples per timestep in a nested loop yields 2h40 per image on an H100, roughly two orders of magnitude more expensive than standard guidance methods. Compute-matched comparisons in the image task are not provided, so it is unclear whether baselines given the same budget would close the PSNR gap.

The tempered-posterior capability (a headline claim enabled by Theorem 4.3) is demonstrated only on toy 1D examples (Figure 1, right); no tempered-posterior experiment appears in the benchmark or the scientific task.

Several technical statements are imprecise: Eq. (20) uses self-normalized weights and is therefore biased for finite K (consistent, not 'unbiased for a sufficiently large number of samples' as stated); consistency of the per-step estimator does not by itself establish convergence of the full discrete-time guided sampler (discretization bias is not analyzed); and the proof of Theorem 4.1 establishes the claim only for small t via a Gaussian approximation, which is slightly stronger phrasing in the theorem statement.

Qualitative black hole figures and the variance comparison (Appendix C) are limited in scope, and no code release is stated, which somewhat hampers reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameter tables.

strengths: The paper clearly identifies and formalizes a real and underappreciated problem: common test-time guidance methods (DPS, ΠGDM-style Gaussian approximations, optimal-control formulations) use inconsistent estimators of the diffused likelihood p(y | xt), so additional compute cannot correct the bias. Theorems 4.1–4.3 are clean, and the accompanying proofs (Appendix A) are careful, including a nontrivial convolution-based argument for the Gaussian approximation result.

The observation that guidance-scale rescaling (Equation 12) is not equivalent to tempering inside the integral (Equation 13) is a genuinely useful and broadly applicable finding — it applies even to classifier guidance (Ho & Salimans, 2021), which extends its impact beyond the methods studied empirically.

The proposed CBG estimators (gradient-based reparameterization, Equation 16; gradient-free REINFORCE, Equation 20) are simple, principled, and consistent, and support non-differentiable rewards. The discussion contrasting the variance behavior of the two estimators (Section 5.3, Appendix C) is a nice practical contribution.

The benchmark evaluation (Lueckmann et al., 2021) directly measures distributional fit (C2ST) against ground-truth posterior samples, which is the right metric for the paper's calibration claims, and results show the expected convergence behavior with increasing compute while baselines plateau.
Limitations are discussed honestly: sampling cost, the weakness of the gradient-based estimator at scale, and the distinction between calibrated inference and reward maximization for natural images.
weaknesses: The headline Bayesian inference benchmark relies on analytic priors with closed-form diffusion posteriors p(x | xt) (Appendix E), i.e., no learned diffusion model. While fast and clean for validation, this substantially weakens external validity for the paper's stated motivation (pretrained diffusion priors); the only experiment with a real diffusion model (black hole imaging) shows the method merely matches, not outperforms, SOTA (26.10 vs. PnP-DM 26.07), at a very high cost of ~2h40 per image.

There is an apparent inconsistency between the theory and its practice: despite claiming consistency, the gradient-based CBG does not converge to the optimal C2ST even at the largest budgets on Tasks 3–5 (0.789, 0.667, 0.852; Table 1). This gap — likely due to variance and discretization error in the inner diffusion sampler — is acknowledged only informally and deserves principled treatment.

A hyperparameter inconsistency undermines the calibration narrative: the paper states 'CBG does not tune a guidance scale since we aim to sample from the true distribution p(x|y) at γ = 1' (Appendix F), yet Appendix G reports selecting γ = 0.003 for black hole imaging. The role and justification of this tuned γ are never explained.

The core estimators are straightforward Monte Carlo applications (reparameterization trick and REINFORCE/self-normalized importance weighting) applied to a known identity; the algorithmic novelty is modest, and the paper itself notes concurrent work (Potaptchik et al., 2026) evaluating the same estimators. The main originality rests on the negative results (theorems) and the Bayesian framing.

Baseline comparability is a concern: hyperparameters for CBG are tuned per task by the authors (Tables 3–4), while baseline settings are inherited from InverseBench (Zheng et al., 2025). Additionally, in Table 1 baselines use learned or approximate diffusion posteriors while CBG uses the exact analytic posterior on these tasks — a structural advantage not isolated in an ablation.

No release of code is mentioned, and reproducibility of the black hole imaging experiment (two nested loops, K = 512, M = 50) relies on unstated implementation details of the inner sampler; the effect of the O(NM) approximation to the O(N^2) procedure on the consistency claim is unquantified.

Presentation issues: Figure 1's plots are hard to parse at print size; the impact statement and limitations are brief; the relationship to DCPS (Janati et al., 2024) — which also performs Monte Carlo updates per diffusion step — deserves a sharper differentiation than one sentence.

strengths: The paper clearly identifies a genuine and important gap in the diffusion guidance literature: existing test-time guidance methods (DPS, ΠGDM-style Gaussian approximations, optimal-control methods) use inconsistent estimators of the diffused likelihood, so no amount of extra compute fixes their bias. Theorems 4.1–4.3 formalize this with clean proofs (Jensen's inequality, convolution/density-ratio arguments) that appear technically sound.

The analysis of guidance scales (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.3) is a broadly valuable insight: tempering must be applied inside the integral over the diffusion posterior (Eq. 13), and naive gradient rescaling (Eq. 11/12) is biased for any non-constant likelihood. Notably, the paper correctly points out this also applies to classifier guidance, which many practitioners will find useful.

The proposed CBG estimators (reparameterization-based Eq. 16 and self-normalized REINFORCE-style Eq. 20) are natural, well-derived, consistent, and support non-differentiable rewards. The variance comparison between the two estimators (Section 5.3, Appendix C, Figure 5) is a thoughtful empirical addition that contradicts the naive REINFORCE-is-worse intuition.

The benchmark evaluation (Lueckmann et al. SBI tasks, Figure 3, Table 1) directly supports the central claim: C2ST approaches the optimal 0.5 as likelihood-evaluation budget grows, while DPS/LGD/DPG/SCG plateau at biased posteriors. CBG (gradient-free) substantially outperforms both diffusion-guidance and likelihood-free baselines.

The black hole imaging experiment on InverseBench demonstrates applicability to a realistic high-dimensional scientific task, matching or exceeding SOTA PSNR (26.10) without computing likelihood gradients, with qualitative results in Figures 6–7.

Good reproducibility: detailed task definitions (Appendix E), hyperparameter sweeps and chosen values (Tables 3–4), algorithm pseudocode, and fair-baseline protocol via Zheng et al. (2025). Limitations are honestly discussed, including the compute cost of sampling from p(x|xt).
weaknesses: The high-dimensional experiment (black hole imaging) only evaluates PSNR, a point-estimate reconstruction metric. The paper's central claim is calibrated posterior sampling, but posterior calibration/diversity (e.g., coverage, posterior width, per-pixel uncertainty) is never quantified in the high-dimensional setting; consistency is assumed rather than demonstrated there.

There is an apparent inconsistency regarding guidance scales: Appendix F states 'CBG does not tune a guidance scale since we aim to sample from the true distribution at γ = 1', and Table 3 lists γ as N/A for CBG, yet Appendix G reports selecting γ = 0.003 for the black hole task. This needs clarification, as it touches on the paper's own thesis about guidance-scale bias.

Novelty positioning relative to closely related work could be stronger. DCPS (Janati et al., 2024) also performs local Monte Carlo updates over the diffusion posterior at every step, and concurrent work (Potaptchik et al., 2026) trains few-step models to evaluate essentially the same estimators (Eqs. 16/20). The paper's distinguishing contribution over DCPS in particular is not sharply argued.

The theorems, while correct, largely formalize intuitive expectations (plug-in/Jensen-type approximations are biased; tempering outside an integral is inconsistent). The theoretical contribution is more a careful formalization than a surprising result.

The gradient-based estimator (Eq. 16) performs poorly on several benchmark tasks (C2ST of 0.789, 0.667, 0.852 on Tasks 3–5, Table 1), limiting the practical value of half the proposed method and raising questions about when the framework works in practice.
Practical cost is significant: 2h40 per image on an H100 for the black hole task (N=1000, M=50, K=512). The proposed mitigation (pretrained few-step samplers for p(x|xt)) is speculative and untested.
The tempering result (Figure 1 right) is evaluated only in a 1D synthetic setting; no experiments validate correct tempered posterior sampling in practice.

strengths: Clear and convincing theoretical analysis: the paper proves (Theorems 4.1, 4.3, Example 4.2 with full proofs in Appendix A) that widely used diffused-likelihood approximations (DPS posterior mean, ΠGDM Gaussian, naive gradient rescaling for tempering) are inconsistent/biased, and identifies the correct form of tempered guidance (Eq. 13 vs Eq. 12). This is a valuable negative result that explains why existing guidance methods plateau regardless of compute.

The proposed Calibrated Bayesian Guidance estimators (reparameterization-based Eq. 16 and REINFORCE-based Eq. 20) are simple, principled, and consistent; the gradient-free variant requires no likelihood gradients and supports non-differentiable rewards.

Strong empirical validation on a standard benchmark (Lueckmann et al. 2021 SBI tasks, measured with C2ST against true posterior reference samples) showing that CBG performance improves monotonically with compute while baselines plateau, outperforming both diffusion-guidance and likelihood-free baselines (Table 1, Figure 3).

Practical demonstration of scalability: state-of-the-art PSNR on the black hole imaging task (Table 2: 27.08 vs 26.07 for PnP-DM), with honest compute reporting (including the impractical 23h DDPM configuration), K-ablations (Figures 5, 9), and bias/variance analysis (Appendix D).
Efficient renoise trick (Eq. 21) provides an order-of-magnitude practical speedup and is empirically validated against full inner DDPM rollouts.

Honest limitations discussion (support-overlap/mass-zero-likelihood caveat), transparent experimental details (full hyperparameter sweeps in Tables 3-4, equal likelihood-evaluation budgets across methods), and promised code release.

The variance comparison between the two estimators (Section 5.4, Appendix C) is a nice non-obvious observation: self-normalization makes the REINFORCE-style estimator lower-variance than the reparameterization one.
weaknesses: Practical cost of consistency is high: the calibrated results require large K (best black hole result: K=65536, ~6h per sample; grad-free uses K=1000 per step on SBI tasks). The paper is upfront about this, but the method is far more expensive than the baselines it compares against at matched wall-clock in realistic settings (renoise K=512 matches SOTA at 2.9 min rather than clearly beating it).

The renoise procedure (Eq. 21) is a heuristic approximation of p(x|xt) using a one-step model; since consistency of CBG hinges on accurate sampling from the diffusion posterior, the end-to-end procedure is only empirically justified, and the residual bias from this approximation is not quantified theoretically.

Novelty is tempered by closely related concurrent/prior work: the authors themselves acknowledge concurrent work (Potaptchik et al. 2026) proposing the same core estimators and a learned stochastic one-step sampler, and Sun et al. (2024) previously showed the tempered-guidance inconsistency. The core idea—Monte Carlo over the diffusion posterior to estimate the diffused likelihood—also appears in DCPS (Janati et al., 2024) in a different form.

The gradient-based estimator underperforms in higher dimensions (average C2ST 0.681 vs 0.527 for grad-free; poor on Tasks 3-5), leaving the practical method essentially the REINFORCE variant; theoretical analysis of when each estimator is preferable is limited to one low-dimensional example.

Natural-image experiments are largely qualitative (Figure 6) or confounded: the super-resolution comparison uses a different prior model (pMF one-step) than the baselines, and the authors acknowledge the numbers are not directly comparable; CBG also trails baselines on LPIPS/FID there.

Minor inconsistencies: Figure 4 caption attributes the black hole task to Lueckmann et al. (2021) while the text credits Zheng et al. (2025); the prompt-alignment experiments use guidance scales γ ∈ [100, 500], which sits somewhat in tension with the paper's calibration/tempering narrative.
Guidance-scale tempering analysis (Section 4.2), while correct, is a relatively straightforward consequence of Jensen's inequality and was already anticipated in part by prior work.

strengths: Clear and well-organized negative results: Theorems 4.1/4.3 and Example 4.2 correctly identify that the posterior mean approximation (DPS), Gaussian posterior approximation (ΠGDM-style), and naive gradient rescaling for tempering are structurally biased, so no amount of compute fixes them. The Jensen-type proofs (Appendix A) are clean and the illustrative 1D figures (Figures 1 and 2) make the failure modes intuitive.

The proposed consistent estimators (gradient-free REINFORCE in Eq. 20 and reparameterization in Eq. 16) are a principled response, and the bias/variance analysis (Figures 7 and 8) convincingly demonstrates that only the proposed methods converge to the analytic solution as K grows.

Strong empirical results on the Lueckmann et al. (2021) SBI benchmark: CBG (gradient-free) achieves the best C2ST among all diffusion guidance methods and compares favorably to likelihood-free baselines, with a fair, compute-matched hyperparameter sweep (N·K ≤ 1e5 likelihood evaluations).

Practically relevant scientific application: black hole imaging with a diffusion prior, including a thoughtful compute mitigation (the renoise trick with one-step mean-flow models) and a useful K-ablation (Figures 5, 9).
Honest limitations section acknowledging the measure-zero-manifold failure mode and that likelihood-over-optimizing methods may win on task metrics; code is promised to be released.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty of the estimators: both are standard techniques (REINFORCE and reparameterization) applied to the diffused-likelihood integral, and the paper itself acknowledges near-identical concurrent work (Potaptchik et al., 2026) that trains proper stochastic one-step samplers for the same purpose. DCPS (Janati et al., 2024), which also performs local Monte Carlo updates per diffusion step, is discussed in related work but conspicuously absent from the benchmark comparison in Table 1.

The headline 'new state-of-the-art PSNR in black hole image reconstruction' is overstated: 27.08 PSNR requires K=65536 and roughly 6 hours per sample, versus ~24–45 s for baselines. At comparable wall-clock the method only matches PnP-DM (26.10 vs 26.07). Consistency with compute is the real contribution; 'SOTA' framing oversells it.

The calibrated-posterior narrative is weakened in practice: the reported full-model black-hole result uses a tuned guidance scale γ=0.003 (Appendix H), and the prompt-alignment experiments use γ in [100,500] — i.e., exactly the tempering the theory criticizes, applied in an ad hoc way. This is fine for task performance, but it undercuts the paper's own calibration story and needs clearer justification.

The practical guarantees are diluted by approximations that break the theory: the renoise construction (Eq. 21) is a heuristic proposal that does not actually sample from p(x|xt), and self-normalized weights introduce finite-sample bias even in Eq. 20. No analysis of the discretization error of the guided ODE (Algorithm 1) is given, so end-to-end consistency of the deployed sampler is asserted rather than shown.

The main benchmark victory is obtained under idealized conditions: analytic priors with closed-form diffusion posteriors p(x|xt), bypassing the sampling problem that the paper's own Section 5.3 shows is the practical bottleneck. The only experiments with real pretrained models (SR, Table 5) trail the best baselines on perceptual metrics and require a task-specific tiling hack that departs from the principled estimator.

The theoretical results, while correct, are relatively unsurprising: Theorem 4.3's tempering observation is already essentially present in Sun et al. (2024), and the inconsistency results follow from elementary Jensen's inequality arguments applied to well-known approximations.

strengths: The theoretical analysis is clean, correct, and well-motivated: Theorem 4.1 (posterior mean approximation), Example 4.2 (Gaussian posterior approximation), and Theorem 4.3 (tempered diffused likelihood, via a Jensen-gap argument with a complete proof in Appendix A.3/Lemma A.2) rigorously establish that common guidance estimators are inconsistent. The observation that classifier-free guidance's gradient rescaling (Eq. 12 vs. Eq. 13) cannot sample tempered posteriors is a useful and broadly applicable insight.

The proposed CBG estimators (reparameterization, Eq. 16; REINFORCE, Eq. 20) are conceptually simple, consistent, and well-derived, with a clear absorption of the prior score into the REINFORCE estimator (Eqs. 17-20). The variance comparison between the two estimators (Section 5.4, Appendix C, Figure 7) is a thoughtful and somewhat counterintuitive analysis (self-normalization reduces REINFORCE variance here).

Experiments directly support the central claim: on the Lueckmann et al. (2021) SBI benchmark, CBG's C2ST improves monotonically toward the optimum of 0.5 with more likelihood evaluations while baselines plateau (Figure 3), and the bias-variance ablation (Figure 8, Appendix D) shows only CBG's bias goes to zero with K. Table 1 covers a broad set of diffusion-based, MCMC, and likelihood-free baselines.

The black hole imaging experiment is a compelling scientific application: new SOTA PSNR (27.08 with K=65536), monotone improvement in PSNR and chi-squared data-consistency metrics with K (Figures 5, 9), and uncurated qualitative comparisons (Figures 4, 11-13). The wall-clock cost trade-offs are transparently reported in Table 2.

The paper is well written, with clear notation, a sensible unified treatment of diffusion/flow-matching schedules, thorough experimental details (Appendices E-I), and an honest limitations discussion (support overlap requirement, measure-zero likelihood manifolds, acknowledged underperformance of image-domain perceptual metrics). Code is promised to be released.
weaknesses: The end-to-end posterior-consistency guarantee is weaker than the headline claim. The theory establishes per-step consistency of the diffused-likelihood estimators, but the full sampler involves outer-loop discretization (Euler steps along Eq. 2), and the practical renoise proposal (Eq. 21) is explicitly heuristic; no result guarantees the combined procedure converges to p(x|y). The empirical convergence trend mitigates this, but the gap between 'consistent estimator' and 'converges to true posterior' should be stated more carefully.

Notable baseline omission: DCPS (Janati et al., 2024), which the related-work section identifies as performing local Monte Carlo updates at every diffusion step, is the method most similar in spirit to the proposed gradient-free estimator, yet it does not appear in the benchmark comparison in Table 1 or Figure 3. Its inclusion would materially strengthen the empirical case.

Only 5 of the Lueckmann et al. (2021) benchmark tasks are used, with no explanation of task selection; margins over the strongest baselines are modest (CBG 0.527 vs. MCMC NUTS 0.553, SNPE 0.545, and the Langevin+REINFORCE baseline at 0.573, which itself uses the authors' estimator). Additionally, the gradient-based variant underperforms several baselines on Tasks 3 and 5 (0.789, 0.852), and this failure mode is not analyzed in depth.

The best black-hole result relies on a guidance scale gamma = 0.003 (Appendix H), which sits awkwardly with the paper's central thesis about the bias of guidance-scale rescaling (Theorem 4.3); the role of gamma here deserves justification. The renoise configuration additionally requires training a new mean-flow model on ~140k synthetic samples, partially undermining the 'training-free' framing.

Practicality concerns: the strongest configurations are expensive (DDPM variant ~23h; renoise K=65536 ~6h per image), and on image super-resolution the method requires an ad-hoc per-tile decomposition (Appendix I) to be usable, then still trails perceptual baselines on LPIPS/FID with a different prior model, making the Table 5 comparison of limited value (the authors acknowledge this). The method's practical advantage is therefore confined mostly to calibrated scientific inference rather than general guidance.

Originality is moderate: the estimators are standard (REINFORCE/reparameterization) applied to the diffused likelihood, and concurrent work (Potaptchik et al., 2026) proposes closely related estimators and samplers; the paper's distinct contribution is the bias analysis of existing guidance and the Bayesian-inference focus, which is real but should be weighed accordingly.
